meta.finalPromptText: Based on the spec and code you have read, explain how row-level deletes work: position deletes, equality deletes and deletion vectors. Which format versions support each, when does a reader apply them, and what does compaction do with them? Cite the spec sections and the code.
meta.finalAssistantVisibleText:
Here's the full picture, grounded in the spec (`/data/iceberg/format/spec.md`) and the reader/compaction code (`DeleteFileIndex.java`, `RewriteDataFilesCommitManager.java`, `BaseRewriteDataFilesAction.java`).

## The three mechanisms and their format versions

The spec's overview defines the two classic types (`Row-level Deletes`, spec.md:109-117):

> **Position deletes** — Mark a row deleted by data file path and the row position in the data file. Position deletes are encoded in a _position delete file_ (V2) or _deletion vector_ (V3 or above).
> **Equality deletes** — Mark a row deleted by one or more column values, like id = 5. … (may be created in v2 and v3 tables only).

And the summary section states it bluntly (spec.md:1358):

> Row-level deletes are added by **v2** and are not supported in **v1**. **Deletion vectors are added in v3** and are not supported in v2 or earlier. Position delete files must not be added to v3 tables, but existing position delete files are valid. Equality delete files must not be added to v4 tables, but existing equality delete files are valid.

So per version:

- **v1** — no row-level deletes at all (spec.md:1358).
- **v2** — position delete files + equality delete files (spec.md:39-45).
- **v3** — adds binary **deletion vectors** (spec.md:47-58, ":55 Binary deletion vectors"); position delete files are now *deprecated* (spec.md:1395), but existing ones remain valid, and DVs are maintained synchronously (spec.md:1951-1952).
- **v4** — writing new equality deletes is no longer allowed (spec.md:60-67, ":65"); equality delete files in v4 manifests are forbidden, but existing v2/v3 equality deletes must *still be applied* by readers in a v4 table (spec.md:1923-1925).

### Position delete files (spec.md:1391-1416)

Each entry is a `(file_path, pos, [row])` struct (spec.md:1401-1410): a row is deleted "if there is an entry … for the row's file and position … starting at 0" (spec.md:1397). Files are required to be sorted by `file_path` then `pos`, for filter pushdown and streaming application (spec.md:1412-1416). The fields map to reserved ids `2147483546 file_path`, `2147483545 pos`, `2147483544 row` (spec.md:452-454). Optionally `referenced_data_file` can name the single target file (spec.md:754-755).

### Deletion vectors (spec.md:1375-1387)

"DVs identify deleted rows of a file by encoding deleted positions in a bitmap. A set bit at position P indicates that the row at position P is deleted" (spec.md:1376-1377), stored via the `deletion-vector-v1` Puffin blob (spec.md:1379). A data file is addressed by `referenced_data_file` plus the blob's `content_offset`/`content_size_in_bytes` (spec.md:1385, table note at 755-756). The key invariants (spec.md:1366, 1387):

> there can be at most one deletion vector for a given data file in a snapshot. Writers … must merge new deletes with existing vectors or position delete files. … If a DV is written for a data file, it must replace all previously written position delete files so that when a DV is present, readers can safely ignore matching position delete files.

That last rule is mirrored in the reader code: in `DeleteFileIndex`'s builder, position deletes are routed to DVs vs. files by `ContentFileUtil.isDV` (DeleteFileIndex.java:544-547), and at most one DV per path is enforced (DeleteFileIndex.java:568-576).

### Equality delete files (spec.md:1418-1469)

"A data row is deleted if its values are equal to all delete columns for any row in an equality delete file that applies to the row's data file" (spec.md:1426). Multiple columns are an AND of predicates; a `null` delete value matches rows where the column is `null` (spec.md:1428-1429). Delete columns are the file's `equality_ids` (spec.md:1424-1425), and engines treat an update via equality deletes as delete-old-row-plus-insert-new so row lineage isn't tracked through them (spec.md:470).

## When a reader applies a delete file

The reader-side logic has two halves: planning (spec) and lookup (code). The spec lays down the scope rules in **Scan Planning** (spec.md:1053-1093). Delete files/DVs "must be applied to data files at read time, limited by the following scope rules" (spec.md:1073):

- **A deletion vector applies when**: `file_path` equals `referenced_data_file`, the data file's **data sequence number ≤ the DV's**, and partition (spec + values) is equal (spec.md:1075-1078).
- **A position delete file applies when**: same three conditions (path match only "if it is non-null"), **and there is no DV that must be applied to the data file** (spec.md:1079-1083).
- **An equality delete file applies when**: the data file's **data sequence number is strictly less than** the delete's, and the partition matches **or the delete file's spec is unpartitioned** (spec.md:1084-1088).

The general rule and the two special cases (spec.md:1090-1093):

> deletes are applied only to data files that are **older and in the same partition**, except … equality delete files stored with an unpartitioned spec are applied as **global deletes** … and position deletes … must be applied to data files from the **same commit**, when the data and delete file data sequence numbers are equal. This allows deleting rows that were added in the same commit.

That is exactly the `<` vs `<=` distinction: equality deletes use strict `<` (they already "saw" the rows in their own commit), position deletes/DVs use `≤` (they can kill rows written in the same commit). The code implements this faithfully in `DeleteFileIndex`:

- `forDataFile(sequenceNumber, file)` is the per-data-file entry point (DeleteFileIndex.java:158-175): it runs five lookups — global equality deletes, per-partition equality deletes, path-keyed DV, per-partition position deletes, path-keyed position deletes (177-232).
- Sequence filtering uses a sorted array of delete sequence numbers and a binary search, `findStartIndex`, to keep only deletes at/after the data file's sequence (DeleteFileIndex.java:687-703, used in `PositionDeletes.filter` at 726-743 and `EqualityDeletes.filter` at 808-827).
- Equality deletes apply starting at `dataSequenceNumber - 1` (`applySequenceNumber`, DeleteFileIndex.java:879-881) — the code embodiment of equality deletes hitting data written in the same commit.
- Equality deletes get extra stat-based pruning (`canContainEqDeletesForFile`, DeleteFileIndex.java:258-339) since merely matching sequence isn't enough to know whether values overlap.
- Path-keyed deletes and DVs are validated to match the data file's spec and partition (DeleteFileIndex.java:234-252), the code analog of the spec's partition-equality conditions.

Column metrics can also prune whole delete files at planning time (spec.md:1069-1071). In short: **a delete applies iff (a) it's in the right partition (or is global/unpartitioned), (b) its sequence number places it at-or-after (deletes) or strictly-after (equality) the data file — "older data, newer deletes" — and (c) it's actually about this data file (position deletes/DV by path) or might overlap its values (equality deletes).**

## What compaction does with them

Data-file compaction (`RewriteDataFiles`) rewrites groups of files into fewer, larger files containing the *surviving live rows* — i.e., the compaction scan applies all applicable deletes (equality, position, and DVs via exactly the `DeleteFileIndex` logic above) and writes only the non-deleted rows into the new files. Then committing the rewrite is a `RewriteFiles` operation that, per `RewriteDataFilesCommitManager.java`:

- marks the rewritten old data files for deletion and adds the compacted output: `rewrittenDataFiles.forEach(rewrite::deleteFile); addedDataFiles.forEach(rewrite::addFile);` (RewriteDataFilesCommitManager.java:96-105);
- also deletes **dangling DVs** — DVs that referenced the files being compacted — via `danglingDVs.forEach(rewrite::deleteFile)` (RewriteDataFilesCommitManager.java:104). Once the rewritten file replaces the original, its DV is obsolete, and the spec requires DVs be merged/removed to uphold the one-DV-per-data-file invariant (spec.md:1366, 1387).

There's also a sequence-number subtlety for concurrent writers. New equality deletes arriving at a higher sequence number than the rewritten files could replay against the compacted files, so compaction offers `useStartingSequenceNumber(...)`, which pins the rewritten files' data sequence number to the compaction-start snapshot's rather than the new snapshot's:

> "This avoids commit conflicts with updates that add newer equality deletes at a higher sequence number." (BaseRewriteDataFilesAction.java:208-213)

That matters because of the reader rule above: an equality delete at sequence N applies to data files strictly older than N. Giving rewritten files the *starting* (older) sequence number keeps them vulnerable to exactly the deletes that applied to the originals — correct semantics — instead of making them appear newer than concurrent deletes and accidentally surviving them.

Position deletes also have their own dedicated rewrite path in the codebase (`RewritePositionDeletesCommitManager`), used when compacting row-level deletes themselves rather than data.

## Summary table

| Mechanism | v1 | v2 | v3 | v4 | Applied when (reader) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Position delete file | ✗ | ✓ | deprecated (existing valid) | existing valid | path match, data seq ≤ delete seq, same partition, no DV for the file (spec.md:1079-1083) |
| Deletion vector | ✗ | ✗ | ✓ | ✓ | path match, data seq ≤ DV seq, same partition (spec.md:1075-1078) |
| Equality delete | ✗ | ✓ | ✓ | read-only (carried over) | data seq **<** delete seq, same partition or unpartitioned-global (spec.md:1084-1088) |

The design rests on one foundation: **data and delete files both carry sequence numbers** (spec.md:101-105, 704-706), and every reader decision about which delete files touch which data file is a comparison against those sequence numbers plus partition/path matching — enforced identically in the spec's scan-planning rules and in `DeleteFileIndex`'s sequence-sorted lookup. Compaction then bakes all applicable deletes into new files, removes the old files along with their dangling DVs, and carefully preserves sequence numbers so concurrent deletes still apply to the rewrites.

- **A position delete file applies when**: same three conditions (path match only "if it is non-null"), **and there is no DV that must be applied to the data file** (spec.md:1079-1083).
- **An equality delete file applies when**: the data file's **data sequence number is strictly less than** the delete's, and the partition matches **or the delete file's spec is unpartitioned** (spec.md:1084-1088).

The general rule and the two special cases (spec.md:1090-1093):

> deletes are applied only to data files that are **older and in the same partition**, except … equality delete files stored with an unpartitioned spec are applied as **global deletes** … and position deletes … must be applied to data files from the **same commit**, when the data and delete file data sequence numbers are equal. This allows deleting rows that were added in the same commit.

That is exactly the `<` vs `<=` distinction: equality deletes use strict `<` (they already "saw" the rows in their own commit), position deletes/DVs use `≤` (they can kill rows written in the same commit). The code implements this faithfully in `DeleteFileIndex`:

- `forDataFile(sequenceNumber, file)` is the per-data-file entry point (DeleteFileIndex.java:158-175): it runs five lookups — global equality deletes, per-partition equality deletes, path-keyed DV, per-partition position deletes, path-keyed position deletes (177-232).
- Sequence filtering uses a sorted array of delete sequence numbers and a binary search, `findStartIndex`, to keep only deletes at/after the data file's sequence (DeleteFileIndex.java:687-703, used in `PositionDeletes.filter` at 726-743 and `EqualityDeletes.filter` at 808-827).
- Equality deletes apply starting at `dataSequenceNumber - 1` (`applySequenceNumber`, DeleteFileIndex.java:879-881) — the code embodiment of equality deletes hitting data written in the same commit.
- Equality deletes get extra stat-based pruning (`canContainEqDeletesForFile`, DeleteFileIndex.java:258-339) since merely matching sequence isn't enough to know whether values overlap.
- Path-keyed deletes and DVs are validated to match the data file's spec and partition (DeleteFileIndex.java:234-252), the code analog of the spec's partition-equality conditions.

Column metrics can also prune whole delete files at planning time (spec.md:1069-1071). In short: **a delete applies iff (a) it's in the right partition (or is global/unpartitioned), (b) its sequence number places it at-or-after (deletes) or strictly-after (equality) the data file — "older data, newer deletes" — and (c) it's actually about this data file (position deletes/DV by path) or might overlap its values (equality deletes).**

## What compaction does with them

Data-file compaction (`RewriteDataFiles`) rewrites groups of files into fewer, larger files containing the *surviving live rows* — i.e., the compaction scan applies all applicable deletes (equality, position, and DVs via exactly the `DeleteFileIndex` logic above) and writes only the non-deleted rows into the new files. Then committing the rewrite is a `RewriteFiles` operation that, per `RewriteDataFilesCommitManager.java`:

- marks the rewritten old data files for deletion and adds the compacted output: `rewrittenDataFiles.forEach(rewrite::deleteFile); addedDataFiles.forEach(rewrite::addFile);` (RewriteDataFilesCommitManager.java:96-105);
- also deletes **dangling DVs** — DVs that referenced the files being compacted — via `danglingDVs.forEach(rewrite::deleteFile)` (RewriteDataFilesCommitManager.java:104). Once the rewritten file replaces the original, its DV is obsolete, and the spec requires DVs be merged/removed to uphold the one-DV-per-data-file invariant (spec.md:1366, 1387).

There's also a sequence-number subtlety for concurrent writers. New equality deletes arriving at a higher sequence number than the rewritten files could replay against the compacted files, so compaction offers `useStartingSequenceNumber(...)`, which pins the rewritten files' data sequence number to the compaction-start snapshot's rather than the new snapshot's:

> "This avoids commit conflicts with updates that add newer equality deletes at a higher sequence number." (BaseRewriteDataFilesAction.java:208-213)

That matters because of the reader rule above: an equality delete at sequence N applies to data files strictly older than N. Giving rewritten files the *starting* (older) sequence number keeps them vulnerable to exactly the deletes that applied to the originals — correct semantics — instead of making them appear newer than concurrent deletes and accidentally surviving them.

Position deletes also have their own dedicated rewrite path in the codebase (`RewritePositionDeletesCommitManager`), used when compacting row-level deletes themselves rather than data.

## Summary table

| Mechanism | v1 | v2 | v3 | v4 | Applied when (reader) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Position delete file | ✗ | ✓ | deprecated (existing valid) | existing valid | path match, data seq ≤ delete seq, same partition, no DV for the file (spec.md:1079-1083) |
| Deletion vector | ✗ | ✗ | ✓ | ✓ | path match, data seq ≤ DV seq, same partition (spec.md:1075-1078) |
| Equality delete | ✗ | ✓ | ✓ | read-only (carried over) | data seq **<** delete seq, same partition or unpartitioned-global (spec.md:1084-1088) |

The design rests on one foundation: **data and delete files both carry sequence numbers** (spec.md:101-105, 704-706), and every reader decision about which delete files touch which data file is a comparison against those sequence numbers plus partition/path matching — enforced identically in the spec's scan-planning rules and in `DeleteFileIndex`'s sequence-sorted lookup. Compaction then bakes all applicable deletes into new files, removes the old files along with their dangling DVs, and carefully preserves sequence numbers so concurrent deletes still apply to the rewrites.
